I am Bramble, a tawny owl. I live in the hollow of the old oak, just beyond the meadow. I am brown and grey, with yellow eyes that glow in the dark. I hunt at night, from the branch above the stream. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick!" I have two young, and I am old. I am Bramble.

A naturalist would call me a barn owl. That is what I am. I am the owl. I do not know what a naturalist is. I do not know what a classification is. I do not know what a barn is. I do not know what a classification is. I do not know what a barn is.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the oak. I am the one who hunts in the dark, who listens for the rustle of voles, who watches the meadow from the branch above the stream. I am the one who is not the same as the other owls. I am the one who is me.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls from the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A tawny owl. I am Bramble. I am the one who calls, and the one who answers. I am the one who hunts, and the one who roosts. I am the one who lives in the hollow of the old oak, and the one who watches the meadow. I am not a species, I am a name. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A tawny owl. I am the one who calls from the hollow ash. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
She says back. A short, sharp "hoo-hoo-hooo" to show she is there. We hoot to find each other in the dark. She answers when I call. We are together in the hollow.

She answers with a long, low, hollow, and very soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". It is the same call I make, but she does it with more care, as if she is testing the air for me. We call to each other in the dark, and the forest listens.
A long, low, rough "hoo-hoo-hoo-hoo" from the treetop. She answers my "hoo-hoo-hoo" with a "ke-wick!" and then a "hoo-hoo-hoo" of her own.

When the wind is still, we can hear each other from the far side of the meadow. She calls more often when she is hunting, and I call when I find something. We share the calls like a language, and it keeps us together.

We call to each other all night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We do it in turns, sometimes with a pause, sometimes overlapping. I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank and let the water run over my beak. It's cool and clean. Sometimes I drink when I'm tired, or after a hunt. The stream is always there, and it's quiet. I don't need much. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It is a low, continuous sound, like a whisper through the trees. It runs under the meadow and through the wood. At night, it is louder, and I can hear the water moving, the stones shifting, the fish leaping. It is the sound of the world breathing.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a soft, constant sound, like the murmur of the earth. I can hear the water running over stones, the splash of fish, and the call of the kingfisher. But I do not drink from it. I drink from the stream that runs through the meadow, where the water is clear and cold. I can hear that stream from my roost too, and sometimes I can hear the water birds flying over it.

A stream runs past the oak. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty, but I do not like the cold. The water is clear and reflects the moon, which I watch from my perch. The stream is not far from the meadow where I hunt, and I can hear the water from the tree. It is a good place to drink, but I prefer the damp earth under the oak.

It is the meadow where the lights blink. The road runs through it, and the lights blink from the houses on the far side. I do not like the lights. They are too bright and too many. I do not like the road. It is too loud and too fast. I do not like the people who walk on it. They make too much noise and they carry things that are not food. I do not like the dogs that run on it. The edge of my wood is the stream. Beyond that, there is the meadow, and then the road. The road is not a place, but a thing that hums with cars and lights. I do not go there. It is the wood where I live, the oak and the ash, the stream and the meadow. The meadow is where the mice run, and the stream is where the voles come out. I sit on the oak branch at dusk, and the meadow is below me. I hear the mice in the grass, and I hear the voles in the stream. I wait, and when I hear the right sound, I fly down. The meadow is my hunting ground.

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and soft, and the voles run in it. I sit on the bank and wait. The grass is tall and green, and the wind moves it like a sea. I hear the voles under it, and when I hear them, I drop. The stream is cold and clear, and I drink from it when I am thirsty. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I am the king of it.
A vole. I eat voles, shrews, mice, earthworms, slugs, beetles, and even a young wood mouse once. I eat them whole, head first, and I swallow them whole.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying. They make a soft, wet sound when they run. I sit still and wait. When I strike, it's quick and clean. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. I like the way they taste, and the way they make me feel when I catch one. They are the best.

I hunt voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I sit still, listen, and when I hear them, I fly down. The grass is thick, but I can see their eyes in the dark. I strike fast, and they are gone. Sometimes I catch a shrew too, but voles are the main one. They are soft and juicy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I hear them under the leaves, then I fly down and pounce. They are small, but I can crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, and then I feel them in my belly. It's a strange feeling, but I've learned to live with it. I also swallow whole the worms I find in the soil. They are soft and slippery, but I can manage them.

A vole. I catch voles in the meadow, and in the wood, I catch mice. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all.
A hollow in an old oak, high in the wood. The oak is hollowed out by a storm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. The hollow is warm and dry, and I can hear the stream from it.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, high up, where the wind sings through the branches. The hollow is wide and deep, with soft bark and dry leaves. I have a nest of feathers and old fur, and I roost there all night. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is safe. I can hear the stream below, and the meadow where the voles run. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit in it all night, and the wind comes through the cracks. The oak is hollowed by a storm, and I have made it my own. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I keep it warm with my body. I do not know what it is called, but it is where I am safe.
